First, look at the little things nobody talks about: the clock, the chair, the height of the table. If someone’s always squinting or leaning, tell the boss, not the janitor. And when you bring in a new chair, don’t just hand it to the guy in the back row. Hand it to the girl who’s been shifting for weeks. Stuff like that.

Then there’s the names. You say “Maria” not “Miss, Miss, Miss, Maria,” and you say “John” not “the guy with the blue jacket.” You remember the right name. You remember the right name when you call the guy with the tattoo on his wrist, not the one with the red one. You don the goddamn name. You do it right, and it’s like a little door cracks open. You can’t see it, but you know it’s there.

You bring the damn coffee. Not the one who forgets, not the one who’s got to ask. I got it, you got it. You remember which one’s too sweet, which one’s too bitter. You remember which one’s got the sugar in the cup, not in the glass. You don’t ask if she wants it hot or cold, you just know. You know she likes it like that.

And when someone drops, you don’t pretend it was the other way. You don’t say “last time.” You say “this time.” You say it loud, so the whole goddamn table knows. You don’t let the clock eat her time, you don’t let him finish his sentence, you just say “no, I’m done.” You don’t let the door slam, you open it wider. You say “wait, I’m not done yet,” even if I am. You don’t let the silence fill up.

And when someone’s late, you don’t say “again.” You say “this time, let’s all go together.” You don’t make them run. You don’t make them run. You just wait. You count the seconds, but you don’t count them down. You count up. You say “wait, you’re not done yet. I’ll be here. I’ll wait.” You don’t move till they’re here. You don’t move till they’re here.

And when someone’s crying, I don’t look at the clock. I look at her. I don’t ask if it’s because of the table again. I don’t. I just sit. I know it’s not her fault. I know it’s not. I know it’s the table again. I know it’s the damn table.

Then I look at the pieces. Is it about the wedding or the ring or the papers? Is it about the kids or the church or the neighbors? Is it about the law or the rules or the noise in the street? If I don’t know, I say so. If I do, I say it plain. I don’ t care if it’s blue or red, just the truth.

But if they want to talk about the kids, I ask who’s raising ’em, and if they don’t, I say, “That’s what matters.” If the priest won’t say it, I say it anyway. It’s not my job to win, just to say what is.

If they ask if it’s right or wrong, I say right or wrong don’t matter, as long as they’re clean and the baby’s got a name. That’s all that matters. But if you want to know why, I’ll tell you, but I don’t get to say it’s my job to fix it.

The entertainment industry doesn’t just play music or show the same old stories—it shapes what people watch, listen to, laugh at, cry for, and remember. That makes it a big deal for what folks think is funny, what’s cool, what’s scary, and even how you say sorry. Here’s how it nudges the rest of us to change our minds about stuff:

First, there’s the words. If a singer’s voice cracks on TV, now everyone’s humming it till next week. If a joke’s wrong, the whole room goes quiet. You start to think you gotta get it right, or else. And the way they say it, the way they laugh, the way they don’t laugh—it’s like you’re supposed to copy it. Suddenly, you’re doing it wrong if you don’t.

Then there’s the stories. If a girl’s crying in her bed and the camera lingers, you think it’s okay to not fix it. If a kid’s got a black eye and they don’t even blink, you know you can’t look. They show you what’s broken and what’s not, and you remember it for weeks. You start to believe it’s real, that it happens all the time, that you can’t fix it. Or maybe you can’t look at it right, so I can’t look at it right either.

And the music, god, the music. If you dance in the kitchen and the radio’s on, you’re not crazy. If you can’t stand still, you’re done. You start counting the beats, you start moving before I do. You learn what’s loud and what’s soft, what makes you stop or go back. You think it’s okay if the whole room goes still, but not if you do it wrong.

And the colors, the clothes, the way they smile at the camera—suddenly it’s you, it’s me, it’s us. You want to be like them, so I do it first. You copy the way they laugh, the way they bite their lip, the way they don’t look at you when they say it. You think it’s a secret, like if you just say it right, it’ll be okay.

And when they don’t show it, when they just turn away, you think it’s not a thing. But you remember it anyway. So you keep forgetting, but you remember. That’s what sticks.

So yeah, the lights, the music, the faces in the seats—they make the world smaller. You think you’re the only one who can’t sleep, or can’t smile right, or can’t say it. But if they did it, it’s okay. So you do it wrong, and I do it wrong, and next time it’ll be right. Or maybe it won’t. But you keep trying anyway.

That’s how the show goes on.

It’s about making sure people can trust what’s real, pay the right way, and don’t get scammed. But you can’t just copy last year’s rules—these things move fast. Here’s how we should start:

**1. Watch how it goes, not how it was.**
You can’t wait for a hundred more coins to vanish before you act. I’ll blink and there’s another one with a new name and a different promise. So I’m watching the ledger, the transactions, the people who keep counting, the ones who don’t. That’s how I know when someone’s fiddling.

**2. Make the addresses real.**
Some guy in some back room says “no one’s ever really there.” That’s a lie I can check. If you see a wallet open, you check it again tomorrow. If it’s still there, maybe it’s real. If it’s gone, maybe it was never there. That’s what I look for.

**3. Give the old rules teeth, but let the new ones breathe.**
If someone hands you a coin and says “pay or I’m done” – I can’t just say “no, you have to wait till the next quarter.” But if someone’s hiding coins in the dark, I’ll know. I’ll check the math, the numbers, the way they move. If they’re skipping steps, I’m not letting it slide.

**4. Watch for the little things that get big.**
Some guy in his room with a screen, counting, counting, counting. He’s got a hundred thousand, then two hundred, then nothing. I see it. I see the panic. That’s when I turn. Not ‘cause I’m fast, but ‘cause I’m looking.

**5. Tell the kids what’s safe and what’s not.**
If a kid’s got a coin, I want to know if it’s real or just a wish. I want to know who can’t lose it, and who can’t find it. I don,’t care if it’s blue or red, just if it’s real or not. That’s what matters.

**6. But I don’t lock the door. I just put the key in my hand.**
If some kid wants to trade, fine. But he gives me the numbers, the way he counts, the way he says it. Not “no, you can’t, you’re late.” Just “how, again? show me.” That’s how you know it’s right.

**7. And I don’t care how he hides it. I’ll find the math.**
If he’s got it under the bed, or in his mouth, it’s still there. I’ll see it. I’ll see it all. I can’t trust the lies, but I can trust the numbers.

So you make the rules, but you write them big, so the kids can read ‘em. And you check the math, not the lips. That’s how you know if it’s real. That’s how you know if it’s safe.

And if it’s not, you take it back. But you don’t just take it from him. You show him why. So he knows next time.

Getting more people to vote isn’t magic—it’s a puzzle with pieces that fit together if someone’s watching. The best approach isn’t just one thing, but a bunch of things, all at once. Here’s what works, and what doesn’t, so you can start somewhere:

**1. Make it easy.**  
If I have to dig through my phone to find the right number, I’m not calling. Same with voting. Give them a card in their pocket, a slip in the bag, a sticker on the window. I’ve got it. Make the forms blue, the lines thick, the names big. Make it look like they’re done before they even start.

**2. Show them how.**  
People don’t trust the machine, so they don’t go. I hold my hand out and show them, “this is the stamp, this is the ink, this is the fold, this is the zip.” Maybe I say it out loud, “three, four, five, done.” Maybe I hold it for them. Maybe I stand there till they do it right. If they see it once, maybe they’ll do it next time.

**3. Put them where they are.**  
I walk in the store and the line’s there. I walk out the door and the sign’s there. Put the forms under the table, behind the soda machine. Put a little sign that says “vote” in red, so you can’t miss it. If you’re standing in the line for coffee, you’ll remember.

**4. Give them something.**  
Not candy, not a thing. But I’ll wait till the last person’s done, then I’m done too. I don he red tie, I hum the song. I say “next.” If you’re not alone, you can count the fingers, you can count the breaths. You can pretend we’re all in it together.

**5. Ask them, but not like it’s a thing.**  
You don’t shout at the table, you just say it, like it’s nothing. “You got the slip, right? You got the pen? Let’s go.” You don’t make a fuss. You just walk with them, like we’re going for a walk. If they say no, I don’t say why. I just nod and go back to the line.

**6. Make it matter.**  
Not the president, not the mayor, not the guy with the blue eyes. The guy who can’t get up the stairs right, the girl who can’t say the name right. The boy who can’t remember, the girl who can’t write. It’s the girl in the third row, can’t reach the table. That’s the one that counts. So I look at her, I look at him, and I wait for the next time someone else comes in, so I can show him.

**7. I don’t care if they win or lose, just come back.**  
If you don’t like the choices, I’ll still hold the door open for you when you come back next year. You keep your hands in the pockets, you keep your head up. You don’t have to be the first, but you can’t be late.

**8. I don’t care if they’re late. I wait. I wait. I wait.**

People don’t come in because they’re scared, or they don’t know, or they forget. So I’m there, holding the paper, counting the dots, counting the breaths. I don’t say thank you, but I do it anyway.

That’s how you get them in the door. Then maybe next time they’ll remember. Maybe. But I keep trying.

So you just… stand there, like it’s nothing. Like it’s just another day. Because it is.

Bed sheets that don’t ride up when they pull their knees in. You know. Real stuff. Real food on the plate, not the kind that’s half gone and the other half in the sink. We write it down, not in the book, but in the air, in the space between the lines. I know it’s hard to see the bruises on the other side of the table, but I do. I see it. So I say it. “Last night, I counted to seven. I didn’t lose it. I didn’t forget.”

The relationship between language and thought has been a big question for centuries. People always wonder if words are just for talking or if they start to shape what you can think about. There are a few different ways to look at it.

**First, some people say language is just a box to put the words in.** That means you think the same before or after I show you a new word for grass. You just remember the color and the shape, not the name. But then, how do you remember the name? Maybe you say it again and again, so you remember the sound with the color. That’s one way you could forget the green, just the green word.

**But then, other times I think maybe the word changes what you see.** Like, if you walk into a garden and I say “dandelion,” you look for the one with the white seeds. I don it’s a different flower, and now I see it. Maybe the word is in my head and it’s there before the flower is. That’s the other way.

**Some people say you can’t think without a word for it.** Like, how do you say “red” if you don’t have a word for red? But then, what about the little boy who can’t say the word but knows it’s red, just from the shade. So maybe the word’s not in his mouth, but he still knows.

**There’s this thing called the Sapir-Whorf thing.** That’s his name, not his face. He said if you live in a place where the sky’s black at noon, you think it’s always black. You can’t see white. The word for white doesn’t come up. So maybe the sky’s white, but you can’t say it. I think that’s not true, but sometimes I can’t tell the difference.

**Some days I think it’s just easier to say the word, so you remember it. But if you’re counting the dots in the sky, you don’t need the word. You just count. So maybe language’s for counting, not for thinking. But then what’s the use of it? Maybe it’s for saying, so you can show it to the others. Maybe you need the word to remember it’s yours.**

I don’t know. Maybe it’s both. Maybe you think in pieces, and if I have the right word, I can show you the piece. But if I don’t, you still see it. But if you’re looking for it, you don’t. I think it’s a game of waiting for the right word to catch up with the thing. But I don’t know if it ever really does.

So, that’s what I think. Maybe it’s not the words, it’s the looking. But if you say it right, it sticks. I guess I’m still waiting for the day I can say it right.

3. ** I remember where I saw it last time.**  
   - If I had it from the city website, I check there first.

   - The one who’s got the paper with the little marks in the ink.

    - If it’s still there, I know.  
    - If it’s not, I start again.

Staying organized isn’t magic—it’s just a bunch of little things done right, over and over. Here’s how I keep it together, and some stuff that might help you, too:

1. **Same spot for everything.** I put my keys under the mat, not the couch. Same goes for the charger, the pen, the mug. Same drawer for the loose stuff, same shelf for the books. Same.

2. **Write it down.** If I remember something has to be done, I write it. Not just in my head. Phone, notepad, sticky, whatever. Then I cross it off when it’s done.

3. laundry goes in the same basket. I don’t let it pile up till it’s a mountain. Monday’s clean, Tuesday’s clean, folded, stacked. I know where it is.

4. I keep the trash out the door. I put the bag right by the bin when I throw it in. If it’s in the sink, I wash it. If it’s in the sink, I don’t let it go back to the counter.

5. I keep my phone in the same pocket. I keep my wallet in the same zip. Same side of the bed for the water bottle. Same. Just.

6. I color code things. Red for the vacuum, blue for the mop. Red for the pens, blue for the markers. It’s stupid but it works.

7. I check the clock. Not to count, just to see if I’m late. If I’m not, I look at the list again. If I’m late, I start over.

8. I put the groceries in the bag by the eggs, not the milk. Then I check the list again. If I forget something, I go back for it. No running.

9. I put the trash out before I leave. I put the keys in the lock, not in the door. I lock the door, even if I’m home for a minute.

10. I don, I fold. I fold the towels, I fold the sheets. I put the socks in the drawer, not the shoes. I put the shoes by the door, not under the bed.

11. I keep a little whiteboard by the fridge. I write what’s for dinner, what’s gone missing. I check it when I open the door.

12. I don’t let the coffee get cold. I don’t let the milk go sour. I don’t let the milk go in the sink. I don’t let the milk go in the fridge, I put it in the cup.

It’s not perfect. But it’s mine. And if I mess up, I start again. That’s the only way it stays clean.

You got a system, not a mess. That’s the trick.

10. I tell myself it’s not a sign, it’s just a thing. Like the rain. Like the noise. Like the way my legs are too long in the morning. It’s just here. It’s not going to get bigger. I keep breathing.

**First, the hours don’t stop.** They stretch, shrink, start at six and end at midnight, or you’re just shuffling another chart, another call, another note. You’re supposed to be here, but you can’t be here, so you’re here a little late, or you leave early and the next guy’s got the same problem. That’s not a fix, it’s a habit.

**Third, the guilt.** You’re supposed to be home, but the kid’s crying and the fridge’s open, and you can’t do it again, so you check the feed one more time. **Fifth, the clock’s always moving.** Even when I’m in bed, I’m counting the minutes till the next call. I’m not sleeping, I’m just waiting for the next thing. That’s how it goes, or I’m dead out here, so I’m not.

But then—some nights, I get lucky. I finish the chart, I close the laptop, I don’t check. I just sit and watch the dog, and I’m done. That’s the only thing that counts. But tomorrow’s going to be different, and I know it. That’s the only thing that’s ever right. That’s the only thing that’s ever done.

1. **Show up early.** Being there before the clock even ticks is the first thing you get right. It means you see where everything goes and who’s really busy. It’s quiet, and you can remember where I sat, so it’s easy.

2. **Don’t worry about knowing everything.** You’re not supposed to. I still mess up the names and the steps sometimes. Just listen, watch, and ask when you have to. The first time you fix it right, you’ll remember it next time.

3. Let them show you how. If they’re moving too fast, wait. If they’re standing still, ask. I used to count the cracks in the floor till I could count five before they let me touch the keyboard.

4. Watch how they write it down. I still can’t tell if it’s a comma or a period in their notes. Pay attention to how they do it, not how I do it.

5. Smile. It’s stupid but it makes the room warm. You get the right answer just by being here, not by being perfect.

6. Ask for the keys to the door. You’ll forget the code and I’ll have to run back with my phone out. Just don’t lock it.

7. Eat something before you leave. You’ll forget I said that and then I’m chewing on my sleeve while I’m counting the minutes.

8. Don’t let them think you’re looking at the clock. I do it every time. But I’m not. I’m looking at the little scratch on the table. You’ll find it.

9. If you don the apron too fast, just take it off. I did it and the lady thought I was waiting for the other one. Just wait for the next one to come out.

10. When you leave, walk out the door the same way you came in. You’ll forget and then I’m stuck looking for the other one.

And if you’re lucky, you’ll get a break and I’ll tell you where the salt’s hiding. But you’ll find it. You just have to look.

You’re not late. You’re early. That’s good enough.

Here’s how the way a boss or manager moves, talks, and does stuff makes the work go faster or slower, and if the right folks are smiling or not.

First, there’s the **tough guy style**—yells, says “do it now or I’ll do it,” and you better run. People get scared, but they get things done. Sometimes. But they don’t ask what they need, and everyone’s tight. If you can’t breathe, you drop the ball. That’s a loss.

Then there’s the **hands-off, go your own way**. They don’t say much, just stare and walk away. You figure it out. If you can, you do it fast. But if you get stuck, you wait for someone else to notice. No one’s fixing it, so it piles up. Chaos. People get used to it, but they don just… forget. Not good.

Next’s the **all eyes on me, all the time**. I’m counting, you’re wrong, you’re late, you’re early. I know where you are. I know who’s breathing wrong. If you mess up, I say it. You fix it. You don’t. You don’t talk. You just… move. You get it done before I see it. But you can’t ask. You can’t say. You can’t say I’m late. I see it. So you don’t. You swallow it. That’s a win for me, but you’re shaking. You can’t sleep. You can’t stop. You can’t stop thinking. You can’t stop. That’s not a win.

Then there’s the **come with me, let’s walk, let’s talk**. We talk about the plan. You tell me what’s wrong. I say, try this. You say no, I say why. We fix it together. You tell me when it’s done. We check it. We check it twice. You know I’m not going to yell. You know I’ll help you. You don’t run. You don’t trip. You just… go. It takes longer, but it’s not my fault when it’s done. You remember how to do it right next time. You don’t forget. That’s the only way you don’t forget.

You just… go. You think it’ll break, but you don’t say. You just keep moving. You get it done before it’s supposed to be done. But it’s wrong. You know it. But you don’t say. So it stays wrong. That’s not right.

Some step’s done, someone else’s next, but no one’s got the map. You’re counting on the guy before you to remember what he said, and he’s counting on the last one to say it right. If you miss, you’re lost. If you don it twice, you don’t know.

2. **It’s all these little things that fall apart.**  
A light switch won’t work, so the window’s open. Then the fan’s rattling and the door’s stuck. You can’t tell if it’s the rain or the wind or the guy who turned the wrong knob. You keep fixing one, and two more go tight.

3. **They’re running out of tape, and the tape’s running out.**  
You got three rolls of tape, but you used two for the windows and one for the floor. Now the box is open and the lid’s on the wrong way. You can’t tell what’s missing till it’s gone.

4. **Somebody’s got it, but not the right one.**  
We lost the keys, but I got the other one. No, you’re shaking the wrong one. No, you’re shaking the one from last week. You keep passing it around, and it’s just there, in the back, under the chair. You miss it till it’s gone.

5. It all comes together or it doesn’t.  
If you count right and the numbers match, you can see it all in the end. But if you miss one, it’s all wrong. You spend half the day waiting for the guy who forgot to bring the thing, and the other half waiting for the guy who took it for a walk. Then you start again.

6. They always find it in the last place you look.  
But by then, it’s too late. The windows are open, the fan’s broken, and the door’s stuck. You’re not mad, you’re just waiting for the next thing to go.

So yeah, it’s not a line of dots on the page. It’s a bunch of dots, and you’re hoping they’re all there. If you’re lucky, they’re in the right order. If not, we’re opening the wrong window again.

---

**1. Figure Out Why I’m Even Here.**
Before I look at anything else, I ask: what’s the reason? New product? Rent’s due, or maybe someone’s walking in the door this time. If I don’t know, I can’t look right. So you write it down, then go back to it.

**2. Find the Right Map.**
I don’t just go to the corner. I draw the lines on the street, see where the cars stop, where they turn. That’s the block. So you find the block, not the whole city. Google Maps, some guy’s phone, whatever. You know the shape.

**3. Walk the Block, Not the End of the street.**
I check the trash, I check the window’s cracked or not, I see if someone’s got a sign up, what’s hanging on the shelf, what’s missing. You count the cars, you count the kids, you count the dogs. You’re looking for the sound, the smell, the way the door’s stuck. You’re not looking for it, you’re just looking. You write it down.

**4. Talk to the people who are in there.**
Not the guy at the counter, not the guy who says “no.” I ask the guy with the dog, the kid with the backpack, the girl with the coffee. I ask what she’s got in her hands, what she’s got in her pocket. I ask what she says when she closes the door. You get the words, you get the pause. You get the look.

**5. Watch what they do, not what they say.**
You see how they move, how they turn, how they scratch. You see the clock, you see the second hand. You see when they look at the door, when they don, when they don’t. You see the sound when they drop the can, when they pick it up. You see the hands, the way the light’s different in the afternoon. You see it all.

**6. Write it all down, not what I think. I write what is.**
I don’t fill in the blanks. I write the numbers, the color, the way the glass is cracked. I write the words wrong, I write the words right. I write it all. You can’t remember the ones that aren the right ones.

**7. Go back. Go back.**
I come back the next day. I come back when it’s different. I bring my own pen, my own notepad. I don’t trust the coffee stains. I don’t trust the sun. I bring my own numbers. I check again. You can’t trust it once. You have to see it twice.

**8. Try it. Try it, then.**
I open the door, I hold it. I put it in my mouth, I don’t. I count how many times I have to say “no” before they stop asking. I see if it’s blue or purple, if it’s heavy or light. I don’t tell you. I just keep counting.

That’s how you see it. Not the way I see it. Not the way you see it. The way it is. That’s the only way.

The relationship between law and morality is complicated, tangled, and sometimes people pretend it’s simple. Here’s what I think you need to know.

**First, what is morality?**  
Morality’s the stuff inside your head that tells you whether it’s right or wrong to steal, to lie, to help the kid on the ground. It’s about what should be, not what is. Some say it comes from God, some say it’s just us, but it’s always there, counting in my head when I can’t sleep.

**And the law?**  
The law’s the lines you can’t cross before they make you pay. Red lights, can’t scream at the kid, or else. Someone wrote it down, someone signed it, and if you don you get in trouble. It’s in the book, not in my head.

**So what’s the connection?**  
Sometimes they match. When enough people cry, they make a law. When a girl throws up in her room, they say it’s filth, not clean. But sometimes they don’t. They could be the same color but different shade. Like, you can’t steal, but you can take my jacket if I’m cold and I leave it. That’s not a law, but I know it’s wrong. That’s just me.

Some folks say law is the only that matters, like it’s the only truth. Others say if you don’t care about the law, you don’t care about the rest. But that’s not true. You can have a law for your hands but not for my mouth. You can put the line in the sand wrong, and the world still knows it’s wrong. That’s not in the book, but it’s in the air.

**So what?**  
They’re close sometimes. They’re far apart other times. If you cut your fingers on the glass, I don’t care if the law says three inches or four. I still stop. That’s not the law, but it’s in my head. But if the law says you can’t, and I see you counting, I’m counting too. I don’t know if I believe it, but I see it. Morality’s the fire, the law’s the smoke. You can’t tell if it’s there till it’s not.

That’s all I got.

That’s a big question—big enough to fill a whole room. But let’s try to break it down. When people ask what should guide human action, they’re really asking about the rules, the signs, the little nudges that make someone pick up a cup instead of the plate, or call someone back instead of just walking away. There’s no book that says it’s right, but there are a bunch of things that seem to work more often than not. Here’s what I think matters:

1. **Looks at what’s real, not what’s supposed to be.**  
If the stove’s hot, you jump, not because I told you, but because I’m pointing and my hand’s shaking. That’s real. So you check it again. You don you’re not listening, you feel it. That’s what matters.

2. **Watches the next person’s hand, not my mouth.**  
If I say “wait” and I don’t mean it, I’m the one breathing wrong. You don’t trust me, you keep your hands in my pocket till the next time I say it right. You look at the next move. That’s how you stay alive.

3. **Wants to be the one who’s not crying when they can’t help it.**  
Not because it’s better for the world, but because it’s better for me. So I grab the towel, I bite the lip, I count to three. I’m the one who’s got to be the one who doesn’t. That’s the only way I get to keep my hands dry.

4. **Wants the next thing to be better than this one.**  
Not for the sky, not for the world, just for the next minute. So I check the clock, I check the window, I check the door. If it’s not different, I don’t even think about it. But if it could be, I keep looking. That’s how you know you’re still here.

5. **Wants to be the one who can say it, not the one who can’t.  
I can’t say it, so I don’t. I wait for the words to come out right, or I just say it wrong and hope it’s close. But if I can say it, I say it. That’s the only way I get to know it’s done.

6. and then there’s the thing about the hands, the eyes, the way you don’t look at the ground when you walk, you look at the next step. You don’t trust the ground. You don’t trust the air. You trust the next step, because if I miss it, I’m not falling, I’m just on the floor. That’s all I got.

So that’s what I think. Not rules, not prayers, just the little things that make you not fall, not trip, not let it all spill. That’s what guides the hands, the feet, the mouth. That’s how you stay in the air a little longer. Maybe that’s enough.

Someone else might say, “no, you have to count to four, or you’ll cut the rope.” But I don’t know. I just watch the next move. That’s what I do.

This is a tough one, and I’m glad you’re thinking about it. Volunteering means something different for everyone, and sometimes it’s just a way to fill a slot, but other times it’s about making the world a little smaller. I don’t know what cause he picked, but I can tell you how to talk about it without making him feel like he’s wrong for breathing the same air as me.

First, just listen. Let him tell me why he wants to go. Maybe he saw a poster, or someone said it was fun, or he thinks it’ll look good on his wall. Sometimes it’s just that. But if he starts talking about the sign, the rules, the color of the tape, whatever. I’ll wait. I’ll let him finish.

Then I ask him, “What do they want me to do? Why do you think they need another person?” I don’t care if I’ve done it before or not. I just want to know. Then I look at my hands and think about what I’d do if I was there, what I’d let myself do, and what I’d say to the kids. That’s all. I don the gloves, you know? I don’t care if I’m supposed to tie the knots or the knots are wrong. I’m not counting. But I check the clock and make sure I’m not late. That’s it. I just do it right.

If he starts talking about the rules, I ask him what the difference is. If he says they want to count to ten again, I say “okay, but I still have to count to ten.” If they want to sing, I hum off key. I don’t say “no, you can’t.” I just do it wrong. Some folks put on these big, bright smiles and tell you everything’s perfect, like they’ve got it all figured out. Some hide their hands, turn sideways, and pretend they’re too shy to look at you right. Others just type in all caps and yell at you for asking stupid questions. And some of them just don’t say anything at all, just stare at their screens and wait for the next thing to happen.

I think it’s weird sometimes, but I get it. You can’t see the way my mouth moves, or if I’m fidgeting or if I’m tired. I don,’t know, forget to say the word right. I wish people would just talk to me like they do in real life, but I don’t mind if they don’t. It’s their world, their rules. I just hope they remember there’s a real one too.

steered:
That’s a big question, and the answer depends on who you ask—philosophers, priests, just folks on the street. But I’ll try to lay out the pieces.

**Absolute moral principles** are the same every day, everywhere. Like “don’t lie” or “break it if you can, then you’ll know it’s wrong.” Some say God wrote them in the sky, or they’re in the blood, or you can feel it in your bones. If you trip over the line, you just know. No arguments, no maybe-s, just wrong or right. That’s the end of it.

But then there’s the world, and the world’s different. A kid’s got fever and he’s shaking, and I know I’m supposed to give him my jacket, not the other one. Or a dog’s got fur in the grass and I know I shouldn’t step in it, even though I could. Or a cop’s got his hand on the door, and I know I can’t open it, not like that. It’s different, and it’s not the same as last time. So maybe it’s not that simple.

Some say the rules are just, and you have to do them, but others say you can’t, not when it’s going to hurt someone who can’t help. So I start counting breaths, and I know I’m breaking the rule, but I’m not breaking it the way they say. So what then? I just… do it different. That’s not the same as not, but it’s not the same as yes either.

So maybe it’s not absolute. Maybe it’s the line, and you stand in it, and if you fall, you get up and draw it again. That’s not the same as never crossing, but it’s not the same as crossing every time. Maybe it’s the shade of it, the color of it, the way it burns when you step in it. Maybe you can’t have it perfect, not black or white, just gray, and that’s all you got.

Some say you have to know, and some say you just can’t. But I think it’s both. You know the line, but you don you know what to do when it’s bent. So I guess it’s the line, and the shadow, and the shape of it when you can’t see it anymore. That’s what I think.
